6/21/26 What's next: Have more time_slots for the longer prime_count values
      We need more time_slots for longer pieces, typically those with higher number of all_primes. When I listen to the longer pieces, the orchestration stays constant for about twice as long as it should. This is the key determining code for the number of time_slots:
            _prime_count = len(np.unique(repeats))  # recovers prime_count: repeats cycles through primes, so unique values = prime_count
            time_slots = int(np.clip(_prime_count * 4, 6, 40))      
      And this is affected by this code:

      Summary of changes in WreckingCrew.py:72-93:

      bass_hold_scale / fp_hold_scale (controls how long each arpeggio/bass note is held, 1–6 clicks): doubled the spread around the old centroid (~1.12). Sparsest level now 2.38 (was 1.75), densest now 0.18 (was 0.65). At the dense extreme this pushes essentially every note to the 1-click floor; at the sparse extreme, most notes saturate at the 6-click ceiling.
      bass_part's internal clip (line 746): widened from (0.6, 1.8) to (0.15, 2.5) — the old clip would have silently clamped the new bass_hold_scale extremes right back to the old range, cancelling out change #1 for the bass part. This was the one place a pure table edit wouldn't have worked.
      FATIGUE_THIN_RATIOS (staccato-chain thinning): widened from [0.9…0.2] to [0.95…0.05], close to the full valid [0,1] range — sparsest level now silences ~95% of eligible chain notes, densest only ~5%.
      Simultaneous-section restriction (line 1802): previously only levels 0–2 restricted how many of the 8 instrument sections could sound at once ((2,3)/(3,4)/(4,5)), while levels 3–5 were all identically unrestricted — meaning density_level 3, 4, and 5 sounded the same on this axis. Now every level has a distinct range: {0:(1,2), 1:(2,3), 2:(3,4), 3:(5,6), 4:(6,7), 5:(7,8)}, so the dense end is pushed toward nearly full orchestration and the sparse end toward just 1–2 sections at a time.

      Changes made:

      3. Start a new python program based on WreckingCrew.py structure overall, but one that is similar to the structure of Partch's Castor and Pollux. From a review of the performance: "In Castor each of the first three sections requires pairs of different instruments and dancers, all three of which have identical measure patterns, but not necessarily the same rhythms. Number 4, then, is the total of these, played and danced simultaneously. Thus, three different compositions become one composition—the “Delivery,” the logical result and the sum total of the factors that make it inevitable. Pollux follows the same plan: Numbers 5, 6, and 7 combined to result in Number 8.”
      I used this scheme in Alpine Daisy - Roof of Wind #28. My blog post: I stole a technique that Harry Partch employed in Castor & Pollux. That piece is structured as three duets, followed by all the instruments playing their same parts together in a “tutti” section. While two players execute their duet, the other four instrumentalists are silent. For the “tutti” they play together. This is done twice, symbolizing the birth of both Castor and Pollux. In this way, you get to listen to the individual parts and to the collection of all the instruments together. It’s very effective in his piece. I hope it will help mine as well. Posted here: http://ripnread.com/sample-page/blog/page/25/. I never really tried the method. Randomness got into the way. 

      4. Work on a video that initially just shows stick figures playing instruments in perfect syncronization with the music. Midi-Motion feeds midi information into a tool that creates the keyframes for the motion in a computer animation pipeline, with prebuilt models for instruments. Wayne Lytle was the musician brains behind the project. He founded Visual Music in 1990. Dave Crognale was the artist who created the models. In 1995 changed name to Animusic.

7/16/26 Ask bob to critique the work of Claude on videos:
      I have been working on a wy to convert numpy arrays of notes into videos. It works by reading @bwv261_features_array.npy and other chorale outputs from @WreckingCrew.py which turns midi files into beautiful fantasias on the Back Chorales using cent tuning that optimizes low number ratios. Here are the latest python programs in a list: bass_section_poc.py
      finger_piano_section_poc.py
      compose_stage_merge.py
      marimba_section_poc.py
      string_section_poc.py
      marimba_poc.py # I'd like to determine if this is the right strategy to create videos of music. The current plan is to show instruments being played by invisible musicians holding string instruments, guitars, marimbas, finger pianos, baritone guitars, and soon to be horns, woodsinds, and bowed string instrumtns for a total of 8 instrument sections with 8 instruments each. I'm wondering if game engines or more sophisitated video tools might be a better approach that matplotlib. What do you think?

      He provided a nice summary of the alternatives: 
      matplotlib vs. game engines for this project
      Short answer: stay with matplotlib for now, and it's not even close given your constraints.

      What you've actually built
      Your pipeline is architecturally sound and more sophisticated than it first appears:

      Data → geometry is deterministic. marimba_poc.build_layout(), string_section_poc.Scene, GuitarScene, TineScene — all compute exact pixel positions from the JI cent data. The coordinate math (oblique projection, standing-wave shapes, cantilever physics) is tightly coupled to your note representation.
      The render model is pre-allocated artists + per-frame .set_*() updates. This is actually the right pattern for offline rendering — it's what animation studios use internally (pre-allocate, mutate, capture), just without a GPU.
      The compositing stage (compose_stage_merge.py's full-frame alpha_composite) is clean and scales linearly with section count.
      Where matplotlib genuinely hurts
      Problem	Real-world impact
      Frame render speed	~0.5–2s per frame at 1280×720 with 4 sections live. For a 75s piece at 30fps = 2250 frames × 4 sections = ~4–18 hours total render time
      No GPU at all	Every polygon, ellipse, and sine-curve standing wave is CPU rasterized
      Memory per figure	Keeping 4 figures alive simultaneously in a render farm isn't trivial
      No Z-depth / 3D	Your oblique projection is hand-rolled; adding true perspective later means rewriting geometry
      Why game engines don't actually help here
      Unity / Godot / Unreal would give you real-time 3D — but to use them you'd need to:

      Export your note data into a format their scripting runtime can consume at playback time (JSON/OSC/a custom asset). Your numpy-to-feature-array pipeline doesn't exist in those ecosystems.
      Rebuild every instrument as a 3D mesh with materials, rigging, and shaders. Your current geometry — the oblique bar projection, the tine cantilever physics, the standing-wave string shape — is all custom analytical math that maps directly to 2D matplotlib coordinates. Porting that to a shader or a rigged mesh is weeks of work per instrument type.
      Drive animation from data at render time. Godot's AnimationPlayer and Unity's Animator are keyframe-based tools, not "execute arbitrary Python logic per frame" tools. You'd be writing a custom plugin/extension to replay your feature-array timing data anyway.
      Lose portability. Your whole pipeline runs headless on any machine with a Python venv. A game engine project is a 2–5 GB install with a project-specific build step.
      Game engines shine when you want interactive real-time 3D with physics simulation. Your use case is deterministic offline rendering of data-driven animation — that's closer to a scientific visualization or a demoscene production than a game.

      The better alternatives, actually ordered by payoff
      1. Blender Python API (most direct upgrade path)

      Blender has a full Python scripting environment (bpy) with a headless render mode (blender --background --python script.py). You can:

      Build instruments as actual 3D meshes with wood materials/subsurface scattering
      Drive animation from your feature arrays via keyframes set in Python
      Render at 1280×720 with Cycles (GPU path tracing) or EEVEE (real-time rasterizer) — both much faster than matplotlib for complex scenes
      Still write plain Python scripts that look structurally similar to what you have now
      The key cost: your coordinate geometry would need to become 3D object placement + bone animation. But the data pipeline (.npy → note events → per-frame state) maps cleanly onto Blender's animation system.

      2. Manim (3Blue1Brown's library)

      Purpose-built for animated math/music visualizations, fully Python, renders via Cairo+ffmpeg. It has better text rendering than matplotlib and a cleaner animation compositing model. But it's still CPU-bound and the 2D constraint is the same.

      3. Pygame / moderngl (direct OpenGL from Python)

      moderngl gives you a Python API over OpenGL — you keep your numpy geometry arrays, write simple GLSL shaders for the glow/color effects, and render frames to an offscreen framebuffer with a GPU. This would be a near-1:1 port of your current math but 10–50× faster per frame. The standing-wave strings and tine cantilever shapes are just GL line-strip draws.

      4. ffmpeg-python with raw pixel buffers

      Skip matplotlib entirely: compute your geometry → numpy RGBA arrays → pipe directly into ffmpeg stdin as raw video. No figure/axes overhead, no PDF/SVG rasterization. This is how demoscene tools work. Fastest pure-Python approach.

      My actual recommendation
      Don't switch tools until matplotlib becomes the bottleneck. You're 4 of 8 sections in and the pipeline is working. The right move is:

      Parallelize the existing render — the 4 section scripts are already fully independent. Run them simultaneously with subprocess or make -j4. If each takes 2 hours, parallelizing gets you back to 2 hours total.
      Add a --frame-range argument to each section script so you can split the render across machines or restarts.
      When you hit 8 sections and render time is genuinely painful, that's the moment to port the geometry to moderngl — your existing Scene.update() logic maps almost 1:1 onto a vertex-buffer update in OpenGL.
      The architecture you've built — pre-allocated artists, per-frame state compute, transparent-layer compositing — is actually the right mental model for any renderer. The switch to a faster backend is a rendering layer change, not a redesign.

      I asked claude:  I'm interested in several enhancements. Perhaps you could assess the difficulty of working on each. 1. Double the resolution vertically and horizontally to improve the appearance. 2. Replacing the vector drawn instruments with photo realistic images from some source 3. Switching to Blender to implement a true three dimensional appearance. I'm trying to reach for what Animusic achieved visually but for my music rather than their cheesy synthetic drek. Their visuals are so amazing I wish I could achieve something like that.

      Claude says: I looked at the render pipeline to ground this rather than guess. Here's the assessment:

      1. Double the resolution — Low difficulty, low risk
      Everything is vector-drawn (matplotlib patches), so this scales cleanly — no re-modeling needed. The trick: W, H, DPI (1280×720×96) are used both to size the figure and as the "1 data-unit = 1 pixel" coordinate system every layout constant is written in. If I just bump DPI, the figure shrinks back to the same pixel output (figsize = W/DPI cancels it out). The clean way is to keep the figure/data coordinates exactly as-is and only raise the DPI passed to fig.savefig() at save time — matplotlib then rasterizes the same scene at higher density, and everything (line widths, fonts, patch sizes) scales proportionally automatically. It's a mechanical change across the 10 fig.savefig(...) call sites plus keeping the duplicated W,H,DPI constants (in marimba_poc.py and stage_layout.py) in sync. Main cost is render time and file size (4× the pixels, so roughly 4× slower renders and bigger PNGs/frames). I'd estimate under an hour of work.

      2. Photo-realistic instrument images — Medium-high difficulty, and I don't think it gets you toward Animusic
      The animation here depends on independently deforming parts of each instrument — a mallet swinging, a bow sweeping, a trombone slide extending, individual marimba bars glowing. A single flat photo can be rotated/scaled as a whole (easy), but not partially deformed. Getting the current level of detail would mean sourcing (or shooting) separate cutout photos per moving part — body, mallet head, bow, slide — at a consistent oblique angle and lighting, which is a real production effort, plus licensing/copyright considerations if this gets published. And notably: Animusic's look isn't photo-based at all — it's 3D-rendered with stylized materials. Photos would give you a different (collage-like) aesthetic, not the Animusic one.

      3. Blender / true 3D — High difficulty, but it's the actual path to what you're describing
      This is structurally what Animusic does. The note-timing/data layer (loading the features array, figuring out when each instrument glows/strikes/bows/sways) is reusable almost as-is — that logic just needs to drive Blender object transforms via bpy instead of matplotlib patch properties. But everything visual is a rebuild: 3D models for every instrument (source from a marketplace like Sketchfab/BlendSwap, or model from scratch), rigging for moving parts, materials/lighting/camera setup, and a render engine choice (Eevee for speed, Cycles for photorealism at a steep time cost — a full ~289s/8679-frame render could go from your current few-minutes to many hours). This is a multi-week-plus project, and the limiting factor is 3D modeling/Blender-scripting skill more than coding difficulty per se.

      My recommendation: do #1 now (cheap, safe, immediate visual win), skip #2, and treat #3 as a separate, deliberately-scoped project — maybe prototype with one or two instruments in Blender first before committing to rebuilding all eight sections. Want me to implement the resolution bump now?
